- If sentiment is positive (≥ 0.3) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is negative (≤ -0.3) or shows recent volatility, model often overreacts to short-term spikes; cap forecast peaks and allow for sharper downward correction.
- After a sharp price spike (forecast > 95), true outcome frequently drops sharply within 5–7 days; model should not assume continuation of upward trend.
- Model consistently overestimates early in the 30-day horizon (e.g., first 5–7 days) — adjust downward by 2–5% for first 5 days if sentiment is neutral or negative.
- If sentiment shows strong bullish momentum (e.g., 0.4+), model often fails to account for mean reversion; introduce a 3–5 day decay factor to smooth out over-optimistic forecasts.
- When sentiment is flat or negative, model tends to ignore downward corrections — apply a downward bias of 1–3% for the last 5–7 days of forecast if sentiment is ≤ 0.1.
- Model often ignores sentiment shifts in the 3–5 day window before a major price drop — adjust forecast to reflect sentiment change 2–3 days prior to major corrections.
